stem.text: In aerobic respiration, ATP is synthesised by substrate-linked reactions and by oxidative phosphorylation.
Outline the process of oxidative phosphorylation.

points.text: releases hydrogen / hydrogen splits into proton and electron ;
ref. to, inner mitochondrial membrane / cristae ;
electrons pass through, electron transport chain / ETC ;
protons transferred, through inner membrane / into intermembrane space ;
proton gradient established / high proton concentration in intermembrane space ;
ATP produced from ADP and Pi ;
oxygen acts as final electron acceptor (to form water) / described ;

explanation.text: Keep electron transfer, proton transfer and ATP synthesis distinct. Electron-transfer energy establishes the proton gradient; proton movement down that gradient through ATP synthase drives phosphorylation of ADP. Oxygen accepts electrons at the end of the chain.

reasoningChain: Start with oxidation of reduced coenzymes.
Trace electron transfer and proton pumping across the inner membrane.
Describe proton return through ATP synthase and the final electron acceptor.

stem.text: In an experiment on respiration, two different populations of yeast cells were used: A and B.

items: Yeast cells in population A had no mitochondria in their cells.
Yeast cells in population B did have mitochondria in their cells.

stem.text: Both populations were provided with glucose in solution and the concentration of ATP was measured every minute for seven minutes.
Fig. 7.1 shows the results of the experiment.

stem.caption: Fig. 7.1
stem.alt: ATP concentration over seven minutes for yeast population A without mitochondria and population B with mitochondria, with both curves and labels.

stem.text: Describe and explain the difference in results between population A and population B, as shown in Fig. 7.1.

points.text: population B produces more ATP (than population A) ; ora
production of ATP increases at a higher rate for population B (than for population A) ; ora
population B carries out, glycolysis / substrate-linked phosphorylation, and oxidative phosphorylation ;

population A carries out (only) glycolysis / respiration in anaerobic conditions / (ethanol) fermentation / substrate-linked phosphorylation
or
population A cannot carry out oxidative phosphorylation ;

explanation.text: Mitochondria provide the stages that increase the ATP yield from each glucose molecule under aerobic conditions. A population lacking mitochondria can still obtain ATP from glycolysis in the cytoplasm, so absence of mitochondria does not imply absence of ATP synthesis.

reasoningChain: Compare concentrations or slopes at matching times.
Relate the mitochondrial difference to the available pathways.
Explain why glycolysis still permits ATP formation in population A.

bullets: Many candidates developed comprehensive and well-focused responses that outlined all the relevant steps of oxidative phosphorylation in the correct sequence and referred to specific processes when describing transport across the inner mitochondrial membrane.

Many other responses, however, omitted details (or included incorrect details) and sequenced the steps in the wrong order. For example, a number of responses referred vaguely to NAD, rather than reduced NAD and described the release of H+ ions instead of hydrogen atoms. A small number of responses incorrectly stated that energy is produced (rather than released) by electrons moving along the electron transport chain. Some responses were confused about the purpose of ATP synthase, often incorrectly linking it to the pumping of H+ from the matrix into the intermembrane space. Many candidates incorrectly named the intermembrane space as the inner membrane space.

Candidates who took care to describe the differences between population A and population B in terms of the concentration and rate of production of ATP were often able to develop effective explanations for the differences.

Many weaker candidates described the data for each population separately and did not make a comparison. Data quotes were sometimes inaccurate and, even when accurate, had often not been selected with sufficient care to illustrate a difference between the two populations. Many of these responses recognised that mitochondria are the site of oxidative phosphorylation but fewer appreciated that substrate-linked phosphorylation also occurs in mitochondria.
